book_title: Becoming Little Shell: A Landless Indian's Journey Home
subject_line: The road to enrollment in Becoming Little Shell
email_body:
Dear Chris,

I've been reading about Becoming Little Shell and how it follows your search for your Métis roots and your pursuit of enrollment with the Little Shell Tribe. It struck me how different that kind of book must feel from One-Sentence Journal, which grew out of such small daily moments.

I'd love to ask how you shaped a personal, sometimes bureaucratic journey into a story about a whole landless people coming home.

subject_line: Sacajewea's own journals, and a museum in Missoula
email_body:
Dear Debra,

I read that The Lost Journals of Sacajewea began as a response to artwork at the Missoula Art Museum during the Lewis and Clark bicentennial, and that the novel imagines journals Sacajewea kept herself that cast her as the agent of her own story.

I'd be curious to hear how that first response to the artwork grew into her voice on the page, after so long since Perma Red.

book_title: How to Commit a Postcolonial Murder
subject_line: Georgie's summer of 1986 in How to Commit a Postcolonial Murder
email_body:
Dear Nina,

I read that How to Commit a Postcolonial Murder is narrated by twelve-year-old Georgie, who, with her older sister, plots against their abusive uncle in a Wyoming oil town in 1986, and that one reviewer called the novel an ode to the state you grew up in.

I'd love to ask about returning to Wyoming after Cowboys and East Indians, and why a child's voice was the right one for this story.

email_body:
Dear Alyson,

In Scribe, after a civil war and waves of fever, a woman trades the letters she writes for scarce goods in the Blue Ridge Mountains where you spent your childhood, until one commission sets disaster in motion. I was struck that you wrote it from Laramie, so far from that landscape.

I'd like to ask what drew you back to Virginia for this book, and why letter-writing became the skill that carries its world.

book_title: Tell Me Everything: The Story of a Private Investigation
subject_line: From fiction writer to investigator in Tell Me Everything
email_body:
Dear Erika,

Tell Me Everything follows the years you spent as a private investigator learning to find and interview witnesses in the case against the university football program, a case that went on to reshape Title IX law. It went on to win the Edgar Award for Best Fact Crime.

I'd love to ask how your work as a fiction writer shaped the way you listened to witnesses, and whether investigating changed how you now write fiction.

book_title: Sagrado: A Photopoetics Across the Chicano Homeland
subject_line: Photographs and poems of the homeland in Sagrado
email_body:
Dear Levi,

Sagrado, the book you made with Spencer R. Herrera, pairs poetry with photographs to document the cultural landscapes of northern New Mexico, and it seems to grow from the same ground as your oral history work in the Embudo Valley and your years as the state's first Poet Laureate.

I'd love to ask how the photographs and poems found each other, and what a camera captures of querencia that a poem cannot.

book_title: Predator: A Memoir, a Movie, an Obsession
email_body:
Dear Ander,

Predator moves through the 1987 film scene by scene, a movie you've watched 146 times, and between those scenes it opens onto your adolescence in the Upper Peninsula and Riyadh, fatherhood, your mother's death and your friendships with men.

I'd love to ask at what point a close reading of an action film became the frame for a memoir, and whether the movie looks different to you now that the book is done.

subject_line: The Angel Island elegy behind West: A Translation
email_body:
Dear Paisley,

West: A Translation began with a commission for the 150th anniversary of the transcontinental railroad, and it answers a Chinese elegy carved into the walls of the Angel Island Immigration Station, while its companion site, westtrain.org, carries the history further through video poems.

I'd love to ask how you decided which parts of the project belonged on the page and which needed the website, and what places like Terrace, Utah, added to it.

book_title: You Would Have Told Me Not To
subject_line: A mother at the bedside in You Would Have Told Me Not To
email_body:
Dear Christopher,

The title story of You Would Have Told Me Not To sits with a woman at her son's bedside after a gunshot wound, and the collection closes with a novella. Your novel You Came Back became the 2020 Italian film Lasciami Andare.

I'd love to ask what the novella form allowed that a story could not, and what it was like to see your ghost story retold in another language.

subject_line: Writing the fractured America of 40 from Boise
email_body:
Dear Alan,

40 imagines a post-apocalyptic America full of obfuscation and rage, a long way in scale from the small-town stories of Volt, and I noticed you discussed it with Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah at the Old Idaho Penitentiary for The Cabin in Boise.

I'd love to ask what made you leave the single town of Volt for a whole broken country, and whether teaching at Boise State shaped how you approached a novel this large.
